title: With Due Respect (Vol. 5) -- Ch. 7: Lessons in Automating Elections
keywords: an overarching need for utter transparency
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5) -- CJP's May 24, 2009 Inquirer column on the 'lessons in automating elections,' recounting how, over 20 years and billions of pesos, the Comelec 'miserably failed' to computerize the 'antiquated, fraud-prone, and super-slow' system -- a failure the Court traced to 'the illegal, imprudent and hasty actions of the Commission'

The three automation phases mandated after RA 8436 (1997) -- voters'-list cleanup, automated counting/canvassing, and electronic transmission -- and the 'three rebuffs' in which the Court voided all the implementing contracts for constitutional and legal flaws

The three voided contracts -- Comelec v. Quijano-Padilla (the Photokina fingerprint deal, whose P6.588-billion bid exceeded the P1 billion appropriated), Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec (the Mega Pacific counting/canvassing automation, awarded 'with inexplicable haste'), and Brillantes v. Comelec (the 'unofficial quick count' the Comelec had no authority to run)

The public-bidding 'lessons' drawn from the Information Technology ruling (which also referred officials to the Ombudsman) -- utter transparency, full consortium disclosure, no unrealistic-then-watered-down specifications, working software, a level playing field, no post-bid substantive amendments, and strict adherence to the bidding rules -- as Chair Melo's team aimed for 'e-hope' in 2010
sub_topics: The cautious chair: the present Comelec, led by Chair Justice Jose A. R. Melo, had 'every reason to be extra careful and to make haste slowly' in procuring automation machines through public bidding, given the body's 'unenviable automation track record'

Two decades of failure: over 20 years and 'billions of pesos,' the Comelec 'miserably failed to computerize' the 'antiquated, fraud-prone, and super-slow' system -- a failure the Court squarely blamed on 'the illegal, imprudent and hasty actions of the Commission' that 'desecrated legal and jurisprudential norms' and cast doubt on its capacity

The mandate and the three phases: after Congress enacted RA 8436 (Dec. 22, 1997) mandating automation, the Comelec -- having postponed from 1998 to the 2004 polls -- split computerization into three phases: voters'-list cleanup, automated counting and canvassing, and electronic transmission of results

Three rebuffs: the Court voided 'all the contracts' for the three stages for 'constitutional and legal flaws,' some bidding incidents 'so stupid and so bizarre' as to suggest 'incompetence or downright corruption'

Quijano-Padilla (Sept. 18, 2002, per Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez): voided the Photokina Marketing Corp. contract to digitize voters' fingerprints because the winning P6.588-billion bid 'exceeded the P1 billion appropriated by Congress'

Information Technology Foundation (Jan. 13, 2004, written by CJP): nullified the 'Mega Pacific Consortium' counting/canvassing automation contract, awarded 'with inexplicable haste, without adequately checking... mandatory financial, technical and legal requirements,' and referred officials and 'conspiring private individuals' to the Ombudsman while directing the Solicitor General to protect the government from the 'illegal disbursements'

Brillantes (June 15, 2004, per Justice Callejo Sr.): invalidated the 'unofficial quick count' transmission of advanced results because the Comelec had 'no authority to canvass the votes for president and vice-president' -- a power the Constitution gives to Congress

The public-bidding lessons: from the Information Technology ruling -- 'an overarching need for utter transparency' (never 'break the speed record' on multibillion-peso contracts), full disclosure of a consortium's 'existence, composition and scope,' no 'very high standards or unrealistic specifications' that are 'water[ed]... down after the bid' (a 'sure indication of fraud'), working software (without which 'the same danger of massive fraud remains'), a level playing field of identical bidding conditions, no post-bid 'substantive amendment' of a contract, and strict adherence to the law and the Comelec's 'own published bidding rules' -- all aimed at the 'electronic, honest, orderly... peaceful elections (e-hope)' Melo's team sought for 2010

stances.claim: The Comelec's two decades of automation failure was self-inflicted: the Court traced it to 'the illegal, imprudent and hasty actions of the Commission' that 'desecrated legal and jurisprudential norms,' voiding all three phase-contracts for legal and constitutional flaws.
stances.rhetorical_move: accountability-by-record: pinning the failure on the body's own conduct via the Court's findings

stances.claim: The three rebuffs each rested on a clear defect -- an over-appropriation bid (Quijano-Padilla), an award made 'with inexplicable haste' on deficient requirements (Information Technology), and an ultra vires 'unofficial quick count' (Brillantes) -- showing the Comelec repeatedly flouted law and limits.
stances.rhetorical_move: case-by-case demonstration: cataloguing the defects to establish a pattern

stances.claim: Honest automation requires heeding the public-bidding lessons -- utter transparency, full disclosure, realistic and unchanged specifications, working software, a level playing field, and strict rule-adherence -- so Chair Melo's team could finally deliver 'e-hope' in 2010, as 'our people expect nothing less.'
stances.rhetorical_move: lessons-as-roadmap: converting past failures into prescriptive bidding standards

notable_anecdotes: 'Make haste slowly': CJP frames the column with Melo's prudent watchword, given the Comelec's 'unenviable automation track record.'
A bid five times the budget: he recalls Quijano-Padilla voiding the Photokina fingerprint deal because its P6.588-billion bid 'exceeded the P1 billion appropriated by Congress.'

His own Mega Pacific ruling: he notes he wrote the Information Technology decision nullifying the counting-automation contract awarded 'with inexplicable haste,' and referring officials to the Ombudsman.

No software, no count: he highlights the lesson that 'the counting machines... will never work properly without the software program,' so untested programming leaves 'the same danger of massive fraud.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's May 24, 2009 Inquirer column, draws 'lessons in automating elections' from the Comelec's long record of failure. Over 20 years and 'billions of pesos,' he writes, the body 'miserably failed to computerize' the 'antiquated, fraud-prone, and super-slow' system -- a failure the Court blamed on 'the illegal, imprudent and hasty actions of the Commission' that 'desecrated legal and jurisprudential norms.' After Congress enacted RA 8436 (1997) mandating automation, the Comelec (having slipped from 1998 to the 2004 polls) split the work into three phases -- voters'-list cleanup, automated counting/canvassing, and electronic transmission -- and the Court 'voided all the contracts' for legal and constitutional flaws across 'three rebuffs.' In Comelec v. Quijano-Padilla (2002), it voided the Photokina fingerprint-digitization deal because the P6.588-billion bid 'exceeded the P1 billion appropriated by Congress'; in Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec (2004), which CJP wrote, it nullified the 'Mega Pacific Consortium' counting-automation contract awarded 'with inexplicable haste... without adequately checking... mandatory financial, technical and legal requirements,' and referred officials to the Ombudsman; and in Brillantes v. Comelec (2004), it struck down the 'unofficial quick count' because the Comelec had 'no authority to canvass the votes for president and vice-president.' From the Information Technology ruling CJP distills public-bidding lessons: an 'overarching need for utter transparency' (never 'break the speed record' on huge contracts), full disclosure of a consortium's 'composition and scope,' no unrealistic specifications 'water[ed]... down after the bid' (a 'sure indication of fraud'), working software (without which 'the same danger of massive fraud remains'), a level playing field, no post-bid 'substantive amendment,' and strict adherence to the bidding rules -- all so Chair Melo's team could finally deliver 'electronic, honest, orderly... peaceful elections (e-hope)' in 2010, since 'our people expect nothing less.'
